newsitem.title: USA: Collapse of barter boosts North Korea food fears.
newsitem.headline: Collapse of barter boosts North Korea food fears.

text.p: Famine-threatened North Korea has cancelled a zinc-for-food barter, U.S. grains giant Cargill Inc said on Thursday, fanning concern over Pyongyang's ability to alleviate hunger after two years of floods.
News of the cancellation came a day after U.N. officials warned that North Korea would have no food stocks left after June 20.
Pyongyang terminated the barter -- 4,000 metric tons of zinc for 20,000 tons of U.S. wheat -- as the ship carrying the grain neared its waters.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said stopping the deal "doesn't seem to make sense from the North Korean viewpoint, if they want to bring more food to their country, and if people are actually starving or severely malnourished, which we know to be the case in certain circumstances."
Burns said the United States was fulfilling its humanitarian obligations by providing food aid to North Korea.
U.S. lawmakers were dismayed by the cancellation.
"I suspect North Korea is in even worse shape than we think," said Sen. Patrick Leahy, a Vermont Democrat.

"Obviously, it complicates the nutrition situation in North Korea further," said Indiana Republican Sen. Richard Lugar, a leading Senate voice on farm and foreign policy. "It's clear they don't have any foreign cash reserves."

Sen. Max Baucus, a Montana Democrat who was in Pyongyang last week, said it was "clear this country is in dire straits." He said North Korean officials told him they were 1.5 million tons short of grain. He said it was clear during his vist that the barter was unravelling -- "I asked why. I got no answer."

Cargill, based in Minneapolis, Minnesota, was given permission last winter by the Clinton administration to pursue sales of up to 500,000 tons of wheat and rice to North Korea -- a rarely granted opportunity that came during a moment of warmer relations between the two nations.
On April 7, after three months of negotiations, Cargill announced it had reached agreement for the swap.
A Cargill spokeswoman said North Korea told the company last week that it "had chosen not to perform. Regrettably, under those circumstances, we will not deliver the wheat."
No reason was given for the cancellation.

Traders in Tokyo said zinc production in the communist-run country was plunging because of floods and lack of electricity to refine the ore. North Korea might not have enough zinc on hand, they suggested.

Catherine Bertini, head of the U.N. World Food Programme, said on Wednesday from New York that the government's food rationing system had nearly collapsed and people faced starvation. Some deaths due to malnutrition already have been reported.

The World Food Programme has raised 144,464 tons of food donations, out of a requested 200,000 tons worth $95 million, in response to the floods. Bertini said 1.8 million tons were needed to avoid large-scale starvation.

Two years of flooding ruined crops and farmland in North Korea. A good harvest, perhaps as large as 4 million tons, appeared likely this year but crops are not mature. Even a good crop would leave North Korea short of food for the coming year.
Lugar said if catastrophe threatened a large portion of the population, "something much larger than what we have been talking about will be needed."
